name: Distrito Federal
summary:
CDMX recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the city's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide made a distinct crime in July 2024 (Ley Paola Buenrostro); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created December 2024 with mandatory 72h/48h action protocols (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025); a new Gender Police with 30 patrol units launched August 2025. Long-standing LGR since 2014, extended to 12-year-olds by 2021 decree. For a visitor assaulted in CDMX, there is trained machinery to investigate; in Nuevo León (0.40) or Michoacán (0.40) there is none.

Modestly above the national 0.55: the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.

name: Nuevo Leon
summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024; five transfeminicides recorded for the year (second only to CDMX). Activists reported six killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category.

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026. A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.15). Versus CDMX (0.57), which pairs similar lethality with a dedicated investigation unit, mandatory-response protocols, and a gender police force, Nuevo León's absence of any transfeminicide offence or investigative machinery is the decisive divergence. Versus Nayarit (0.57), which was first in the country to typify the crime in 2024, Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

name: Michoacan de Ocampo
summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026). Six LGBT homicides recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia (suspect arrested — a positive institutional response). Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026 were linked by the attorney general to organised crime. The state's own official locates most attacks in Tierra Caliente, a comarca under armed-group influence, while a civil-society count attributes 102 killings of gay men to named municipalities between 2015–2024.

Activists report victims are no longer attended to and the violence is not acknowledged by the state. The arrest in the Daniela case is a single positive data point against a backdrop of collective non-acknowledgment. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.15). Versus Veracruz (0.42), which at least has a gender-identity civil-code reform (2025), Michoacán lacks even that; its armed-group amplifier in Tierra Caliente and border-with-Jalisco escalation make the violence pattern harder to escape. Versus CDMX (0.57), where a dedicated unit and mandatory-response protocol exist, Michoacán has no legal machinery whatsoever.

name: Quintana Roo
summary:
For a transgender visitor specifically, this is the most directly relevant state in Mexico: the tourist corridor of Cancún, Tulum and Playa del Carmen is where visitors go and where documented policing failures concentrate. Municipal and state police have repeatedly committed discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people, with multiple recorded assaults during detention concentrated in Tulum and Playa del Carmen. The Transgender Law Center's country report documents officers dragging trans women by the hair and using arrest to extract extortion payments and sexual favours — a state-implicated pattern. Two Tourist Police officers in Cancún were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors using portable card terminals, confirming the tourist-facing police layer itself is a risk. The Cancún INM immigration detention facility is documented as a site of systematic rights violations with no accountability.

Countervailing: Quintana Roo enacted LGR in 2020, banned conversion practices in December 2023, recognised transfeminicide, and the Cancún hotel zone is commercially welcoming to LGBTQ+ tourists. These are positive but do not protect a visitor from police detention or extortion, which is the primary documented mechanism of harm here.

Below the national 0.55 (−0.13). Versus CDMX (0.57), which pairs worse raw violence with dedicated investigative machinery and a gender police force, Quintana Roo's problem is inverted: lower lethality but higher probability of state-implicated harm at the exact point where a visitor encounters police. Versus Nayarit (0.57), which shares the protective statutes but has no documented policing failure, the enforcement gap is decisive.

name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
summary:
Veracruz led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years (2021: 10 recorded violent deaths). In 2025, at least 15 hate crimes were recorded; a running total of 460 unresolved hate-crime cases was reported in January 2025. Activists cite 'rezago y archivamiento de expedientes' (deliberate filing and archiving of cases); the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely. Emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences. The 2025 murder of 'Luis M' in an Oluta motel continued the pattern, with the state observatory counting 9 hate crimes earlier that same year.

The only institutional counterweight is recent: Veracruz passed its gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025 (no age limit), the second-to-last of the 22 legislating states. Before that, a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct documents. The absence of any functioning investigation or prosecution machinery — distinct from other states where laws exist but enforcement is weak — makes the impunity here total.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.13). Versus Guanajuato (0.53), which also carries sustained violence but has a comprehensive diversity law and court-forced recognition procedure, Veracruz's four-year lethality record combined with explicit case-archiving and lost files represents the worst enforcement climate. Versus Nayarit (0.57), which typified the offence first in the country, Veracruz's legal framework arrived latest and is least functional.

name: Oaxaca
summary:
In May 2024, the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer 'Goola' in Juchitán circulated a written invitation stating 'men dressed as women will not be admitted.' Muxe activists including poet-lawyer Elvis Guerra filed a CONAPRED discrimination complaint, saying 'this is not the muxe paradise.' These festivals are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists, making the exclusion directly visitor-facing. The state human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 discrimination investigations involving LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. April 2025 reporting characterised Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist paradise but 'the most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community,' with incidents under investigation for possible municipal-police participation in regions where armed groups operate. Authorities responded by stepping up visitor security.

Countervailing: LGR since 2019, extended to 12+ in 2021, fully opened by a 2023 Supreme Court ruling. Traditional muxe recognition is culturally real (49th annual 'Auténticas Intrépidas Buscadoras del Peligro' vela). The positive and negative signals coexist: the formal legal framework is protective, but customary-exclusion enforcement at the exact events tourists attend, combined with the 'most dangerous' characterization, creates a specific travel risk.

Below the national 0.55 (−0.07). Versus Yucatán (no record, ~national), which has a 23-year uninterrupted Pride march and no documented counter-attacks, Oaxaca's tourist-facing exclusion and armed-group amplifier are materially worse. Versus CDMX (0.57), where the same high violence is met with a dedicated investigation unit and protocol, Oaxaca's violence is attributed partly to police participation and addressed by 'stepping up visitor security' rather than structural reform.

name: Puebla
summary:
Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 reporting states. Its LGR law (2021) imposed an 18-year-old requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents need to match presentation.

No dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, no state-level enforcement data. The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes; here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling.

Below the national 0.55 (−0.10). Versus CDMX (0.57), which also had high 2024–25 counts but created a transfeminicide unit and protocol within months, Puebla has neither the legal correction nor any enforcement innovation. Versus Estado de México (0.48), which also defies a SCOTUS ruling on recognition but at least has hate-crime provision art. 211 Sexies since 2021, Puebla has neither the court-compliance nor the criminal-law protection.
